title: Efficient approximation of the optimal dihedral measurement
formal: Can the specific pretty good measurement \(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{N-1},E_{\bot}\}\) defined below be approximated by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits to every requested inverse-polynomial accuracy? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic circuit generator and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), number of copies \(k\ge1\), and precision parameter \(m\ge2\), it runs in time at most \(p(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+k+m)\) and produces a circuit with at most that many gates and ancilla qubits whose output distribution satisfies \[\sup_{\sigma}\frac12\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z_N\cup\{\bot\}}\left|\Pr[C_{N,k,m}(\sigma)=j]-\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\right|\le\frac1m?\] The supremum ranges over all input density matrices on \((\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The circuit receives one such state and returns one classical outcome. The selected target concerns this concrete measurement, without requiring a particular unitary realization or a Subset Sum algorithm.

source_formulation.text: Can the optimal dihedral measurement be implemented efficiently without requiring the known coherent subset-sum-sampling construction?

why: This isolates the cost of extracting the information already present in dihedral coset states. An efficient implementation would turn a provably optimal measurement into an algorithmic resource, while a general impossibility theorem would distinguish measurement optimality from computational feasibility.
status_note: Source-open implementation question with the user-authorized measurement target and explicit approximation conventions. On 16 September 2026 the TQC 2016 source, full original measurement §§4–5 and §8, later survey §6.4, August 2026 restricted-family abstract/introduction and bounded later-work searches were checked. No uniform polynomial-size approximation meeting the stated full-input distribution guarantee, or general nonexistence theorem, was identified. Restricted coherent-implementation hardness is not claimed for all POVM realizations. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

sentences: The selected question asks for efficient approximation of one explicitly defined optimal quantum measurement.
Its input space contains several dihedral coset-state registers, and its outcomes are candidate hidden shifts plus a complementary outcome.
The measurement is defined by the inverse square root of the sum of the ensemble states, with an explicit convention on its kernel.
The required circuit must reproduce its outcome distribution uniformly on valid inputs to any requested inverse-polynomial accuracy.
Known subset-sum connections constrain particular unitary implementations and do not establish hardness for every measurement circuit.

definitions:
Write \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), with addition modulo \(N\). For a hidden shift \(s\in\mathbb Z_N\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z_N\), let \[|c_x^{(s)}\rangle=\frac{|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad \rho_s=\frac1N\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_N}|c_x^{(s)}\rangle\langle c_x^{(s)}|.\] Thus \(\rho_s\) is the mixed state obtained by a uniform unknown coset offset. For \(k\) independent samples with the same shift, the state is \(\tau_s=\rho_s^{\otimes k}\) on \(\mathcal H_{N,k}=(\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The discrimination ensemble assigns prior probability \(1/N\) to each shift \(s\). Both this prior and the average over coset offsets are part of the definition; neither \(s\) nor the offsets are supplied to the implementing circuit.

For this ensemble define \[G=\sum_{s\in\mathbb Z_N}\tau_s,\qquad E_s=G^{-1/2}\tau_sG^{-1/2},\qquad E_{\bot}=I-P_G.\] The inverse square root is the inverse on the support: if \(G=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda\) is its spectral decomposition, then \(G^{-1/2}=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1/2}P_\lambda\), with value zero on the kernel, and \(P_G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda\). Every \(E_s\) is positive semidefinite and \(\sum_sE_s=P_G\). Adding \(E_{\bot}\) makes the sum the identity on the entire input space. A positive operator-valued measure is such a finite collection of positive semidefinite operators summing to identity; its outcome probabilities on state \(\sigma\) are \(\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one. Hermitian means \(\sigma=\sigma^\dagger\), with dagger conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\sigma v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\). The above expression, including its kernel convention, fully specifies the measurement even when \(G\) is singular. On each \(\tau_s\), outcome \(\bot\) has probability zero. The source associates that complementary outcome with the trivial hidden subgroup, but optimality is asserted for the uniform ensemble of order-two subgroups.

The classical generator receives \(N\) in binary and \(k,m\) in unary. This makes the error tolerance \(1/m\) and the polynomial dependence on its reciprocal explicit. The target does not demand polynomial dependence on \(\log m\). Each \(N\)-dimensional register is embedded in \(q=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\) qubits by the binary basis encodings of \(0,\ldots,N-1\); the input therefore uses \(k(q+1)\) qubits. No correctness condition is imposed on states outside that valid encoded subspace. The given state can be mixed, entangled across copies, and unrelated to an actual hidden shift; the error bound specifies the measurement on its whole valid input space. The circuit receives no further copies or a state-preparation oracle. It may consume the input, and no condition is imposed on the remaining quantum state after it outputs the label. In particular, this is a guarantee for classical outcome distributions, not for a prescribed post-measurement state or a particular coherent circuit extension.

Ancillas start in zero, and the circuit uses the fixed gates \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] These act on the indicated wires and as identity elsewhere; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two and \(i^2=-1\). A final computational-basis measurement produces a binary outcome label, with \(0,\ldots,N-1\) interpreted as shifts and every remaining label mapped to \(\bot\). Ordinary finite gates and classical bit operations have unit cost, so no arbitrary real matrix is supplied as one free gate. There is no nonuniform advice, extra oracle, postselection or unbounded repeat-until-success loop. The displayed half-sum is total variation distance between the actual and specified outcome distributions; it is the largest difference in probabilities of an event defined by a set of labels. The requirement is uniform in the input state and every finite \(N,k,m\), with one polynomial and generator for the whole family. It asks for a sample from the distribution, not an explicit list of its \(N+1\) probabilities.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the displayed uniform approximation family exists, including the circuit-generation and gate bounds and its total-variation guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such polynomially bounded family exists. A negative proof must cover all implementations of these outcome probabilities, not merely a prescribed subset-sum-basis unitary or a chosen extension to a larger Hilbert space. A different measurement with a good success probability for recovering the hidden shift does not by itself implement the specified POVM. Agreement only on the average success rate, or only on the coset ensemble without the uniform-input error guarantee, is insufficient for this precise implementation target. Exponential dependence on \(\log N\), \(k\), or the unary precision parameter does not meet the resource bound. This is a yes/no efficiency question with accuracy quantified in its definition, not a numerical output problem requiring only a fixed additive tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The imported card combined implementation of an optimal measurement with the broader relation between the dihedral problem and random Subset Sum at different densities. On 16 September 2026 the user selected efficient approximation of the specific measurement. The present target records that narrowing and explicitly fixes its statistical error criterion and unary inverse-accuracy parameter. The wider reduction question is not claimed answered.

Bacon, Childs and van Dam prove that the displayed pretty good measurement maximizes the probability of identifying a uniformly random hidden shift from the coset-state ensemble. Optimality is an information-theoretic statement: it does not bound the number of elementary gates needed to carry out the measurement.

Their Theorem 2 gives success probability at least \(1/8\) once \(k\ge\log_2N+4\), and bounds it above by \(2^k/N\) for every \(N,k\). Thus enough copies can contain useful information even while extracting that information efficiently remains difficult. The chosen implementation target permits all copy counts and does not select a random Subset Sum density.

The earlier implementation analysis connects coherent uniform sampling of subset-sum solutions with an implementation of the optimal measurement. Its converse imposes a particular refinement and unitary realization. The 2016 source studies further restricted types of subset-sum-basis unitaries and derives consequences for subset-sum collision problems. Those statements do not prove a lower bound for every possible circuit with the same measurement statistics.

The later dihedral survey continues to separate the existence and success rate of an optimal measurement from its efficient implementation. Its exact-recovery no-go statements concern deterministic recovery from nonorthogonal samples, not approximation of the probabilistic measurement defined here.

The August 2026 semidirect-product algorithms apply under explicit restrictions on the abelian factor and the acting prime. For the dihedral action that prime is two, and the required ratio condition does not cover arbitrary cyclic order. Those results therefore do not supply this general measurement implementation.
